speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: A lot of that he knows. Christ, they haven't put any content, his dad knew about that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well what was the story, the way you heard it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well he heard it, he wrote back to Minnesota and told them about when he drove into Troy with the hack, when he crossed the Spring Valley Creek there, the fish were addicted to get his hack called Fish. That's all I heard, I heard that when I was a kid.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard one other one, he used to say, they asked him about the hills, and they said well it's hilly out there isn't it, because it's flat in Minnesota, and he said well, but all the hills run down, so there's no trouble with that.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, they heard that when you go coasting, but they didn't see him coming back up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about Magnus and Johan Johansen, those two brothers, what do you remember about them? I heard they did a lot of things alike.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They lived up here north, you know what Clark Gipper was, they lived north. Well Hunt, Hunt owned the land.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember them doing a lot of things together in the old days?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: All I know is, you see them in town together, and when they had a corn crop pipe in one light, the pipe the other one filled up in the other light the same way. Then they'd see me in church, we went to church there, we'd see them in church every Sunday.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard that they...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: That's all I know, they really got along well. They were just a pair, when the first one died, he passed away in the street, he was in the sermon in the church over there. See that hall down there by the park? Well that's the Old Norse church. That used to be where Addie Swanson, you leave Addie and go up a little hill and around the curve. Well right in on Toon's Field there, that's where the church sat and they moved from there to Troy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That was the church everybody went to?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, that's where everybody went to.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So he died in the middle of the sermon, eh?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: And his brother, he got to his plum loss from there. That was Magnus that died in church.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've seen their graves right next to each other in the cemetery. I'd heard from Carl, he said that they sold their place, you know, and then they were really sorry and they went back to it almost every day to look at it. Well, they had to go back and see it and finally they got it back again.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh, that's what he said. Oh, I didn't know anything about that. I know that after Magnus died, then the church master, the young he lived in, probably lived up west down here in Mandel's Rest Home, right next to the National Church there where they tore that old building down. That's where he was the last.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This guy that I said before was, and you didn't know him, I think I said his name was Wild Bill, but what I've heard is that his name is Wild Davey and that he wore a buckskin jacket around the country a lot. Do you remember anything about it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Wild Davey. I'll tell you that once before more time. Or if I was, I guess I was born, but I was just a little kid. I don't even remember seeing him. I just rather heard about him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you hear about him? That there was a guy that had...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yes, see he lived, he had to dug out something like that, all of it down here on this side of Kendrick. And he had to dug out in the rocky side hill over there in the Boulder Creek Canyon.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear he had a lot of dogs?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: A lot of dogs, yeah. He had a lot of dogs all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear anything else about him? Like what he used to do?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: The whole thing you sort of heard, you know, they said he'd always had a pine squirrel tail and a hawk feather in his hat. Always had a white-brimmed hat. My half-brother, he knew him. He didn't know him, but he seen him. It's too bad like some of them old, like old Alfred Mattson, if he be living now. He always come over there when he come over to the creek. He'd stop there, go on and stop there. After he come back from Troy, he would Moscow day to go there. No Troy, he said they were Moscow day trading. And then he always stay overnight over there. He stay overnight on Boulder Creek? No, over here on the Mattson. Oh, I see. Archibald's place, no. Oh, you mean Davy Wood? No. You know? Is he out of... Carl, I bet you Carl, he's always... Carl should remember.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He remembered a little bit about him. He told me, he was the first guy that told me about him. He said he used to, he said he was a great hunter. While Davy did, he liked to shoot the bull.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Not like Joe Bjergland, he should know about him because he had come by there when he went from Boulder Creek to Moscow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever hear about this, there was a miner who lived on Boulder Creek or down around Park? I heard from a couple people, there was a sort of a foolish miner out there. He was a guy who dug around, he dug a lot of holes and didn't ever get anything. But you never heard of him, anything?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No. I didn't know of anybody prospecting down in there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about Marshall Hayes? What have you heard about him?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, I'll tell you, there's another one that happened. I wasn't... I guess I could have been over six years old when he got killed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear... well I know, I mean a lot of these things like this, I mean they're beyond what most people are old enough to remember. I mean everybody that was old enough to 15 or better or 20 at that time, they're mostly all dead. But I was wondering what you heard about what happened in the business.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I knew that he was copying Troy and then at the slide he shot him. I don't know what came up between them, I don't know what that shooting was about.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: The one that Billy McGinn, now Todd McGinn might know something from his dad there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think so?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, because Billy McGinn, he was in the livery barn during the shooting. He dug back in the livery barn. He used to drive the livery team for Jones down there. So Billy McGinn, he told me that he was there at the time. See one was up the street and one was in the livery barn. And they had a big sign there in the corner, Inland Hotel. And that was taken down here, it can't be over seven years ago. And I never looked until a while before Billy McGinn died, he told me, well you seen the bullet hole? No, I said it. And they had taken that sign, there were seven bullet holes shot up in that sign. Really? Shot that high.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who was that? Was that Sly?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: That must have been Sly.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well see I'd heard that Sly wanted to get Hayes' sons after he got Hayes. That Hayes' sons were going after Sly. And that's why the shooting, he was shooting down on the street.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I don't know what the trouble was about that. You smoke?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: No, no, Harvey didn't.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Before that, I know old Chuck Wells up here, the Negro, he tried to arrest him there in Troy. Chuck was drunk and he'd be on the side of the road, right out of town. And he chased them clean to the top of the hill that were way down in there, to where the trailer house on the back road out of Troy. And kept shooting at old Chuck Wells. Oh not Chuck, Joe, Joe Wells. Kept shooting at him there too. Then he hollered back, he says, sir, it'll be my time next. Next time it comes Troy, then Sly will try to say, oh, it's too bad. He says, I don't want that chance. Because he figured out shooting him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So Joe stood up to him, eh? Joe stood up to him.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He stood up to him in town, but then after he got on his horse and started out, then he started shooting at him. What they said then, there was the storekeeper, I don't know, Larsen or Olaf Olsen had the store there with the bus depot. And told him if he'd shot Joe Wells there, he'd have had it because he didn't have the right to shoot at him. I mean, it's good enough to get out of the horse and leave town. I'll tell you, I think it really was kind of, might have been. You know over there right across from the depot is them old houses back in there. That's nothing but cat houses. And old Yoyos would go down there. Or he's too. So I just wanted to start over with some drinks and a brawl there. I don't know, I never heard.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you ever heard of Joe fighting anybody?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It was liked around here. I'll tell you if you'd have picked on Joe, you'd have had a bunch on you. Same with Chuck Wells. I'll tell you Chuck was a well-liked New Winston. There was no use starting an argument with Chuck or you'd have everybody else on you. He was just considered the best white man in the world.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's really good.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I worked around him, for Christ's sake. He was always laughing. He was just like your dad, always laughing, happy. He was full of fun.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever meet Lou Wells, Joe's wife?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No. I seen her. I've been there, he's got a tobacco shop there in Deary. I seen an old lady, but that's all. Don't even remember her, but she's kind of a skinny woman.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Arthur Burke, you know him? He told me once, he said, Joe used to like to say, I like my whiskey, but Lou, she likes her tobacco. And he said she used to like to chew tobacco.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: She liked her tobacco.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: In fact, he said she used to spit it through the knot holes of the old log cabin. She was that good.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You know? No, I don't remember. I can't remember. Chuck, he started getting... He was a very dark. And his inside of his head was plumb white.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Joe, he used to freight too, didn't he? I heard he used to haul stuff.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, he could have. He done logging, I think, up around there, around Deary.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You told me he was a really strong man, Joe.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, he was strong, and Chuck was stronger.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Stronger than Joe?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh boy. That was the man of his powerhouse right there. He used to keep him on the landing, rolling back, and he was getting him with horses to roll back, and he left the skidways. He had a hard time keeping Peavey handles for him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This is Chuck now.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He break the Peavey handles. I know he... I heard about it. My brother-in-law worked up at Camp 14 for Frank Jean. And he found a line in there, and a big pine log, probably three feet and better than two. And he'd go and roll them logs, and he'd break Peavey handles. And Chuck was strong. I seen Chuck. When I was at the powerhouse. You know, first I worked in the woods. Oh, thank you. I met Chuck then. He was married then. His first wife, Milbert, the one that married Dan Ross, Mrs. Ross. She was Mrs. Ross when she died. That was his first wife. Yeah, them dirty people, they should know a lot about them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: About Joe.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: The whole family married, the daughter, nigga married, they called her. And her two children, they should know about them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about what you heard about, oh, Vollmer and the hard times in 93? Did you ever hear talk about Vollmer, the guy that the town of Troy was named before he...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, Vollmer, that was the first town, you know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: More about the man. I heard he owned a lot of, or he got a lot of land in here during the, well, a lot of places.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He might have had a lot of land, but the first flour mill down at Driscoll's, that was Vollmer's milling company. And then after that, I don't know what it was, then he went down on the coast. But you see, at that time, where Vollmer was, I wasn't even here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Never even thought of you.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No, I was born in Vollmer, I don't know. It was still Vollmer when I was born.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I want to ask you about the thrashing, too, and about what that was like. You're telling me that the Olsons ran a real good thrashing operation, and I know Carl, you know, he would never just tell me that they did a real good job, because he wouldn't say that about himself. But you told me that they did do really good work, is that right?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You bet. Carl and Oscar. Oscar, Carl was the engineer and Oscar was the separate tenderer. Boy, I'll tell you, if we could do it, then Oscar could do it. And I'll tell you, another one was Albert, who died in Moscow, and Roberts had passed away in Troy. They had a thrashing outfit together. There were two other good thrashmen, but I'd say Oscar had everybody beaten. Like Amel said, there's none in the family that could beat Oscar.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say that about how if it could be thrashed to Oscar, you mean if it was dry enough or what?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: If it was dry enough and could be held, Oscar would set the machine to do it. And he'd always check in the store behind to, on the shaft for two season, nothing's going over.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they work fast?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They worked fast. Oscar could set the machine so it would take a lot of grain. He set his sieve and shaft for so that it would take it. What did they try to do? I'd like it now when they're out on the ridges there. Well, I showed you that calendar of Carl and Oscar, you know, all them sacks in that ten-hour trashing out there. The fourth brothers, 1924. That was Oscar, the separator man. And then he trained Amel with him. So Amel worked with him every year by half-oil and ten separators. And Amel, I'll tell you, is a good thrashman too. Yeah, Amel could thrash.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you work on the crews up here at all? Did you work with them?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, the only thing, you know, they come around here. Well, they need so many bundled teams, the farmers go together and help each other out. Right. That's how I worked with them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you work from dawn till dark? Or how did it go?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh, you know, we put in 12 hours. 12 hours actually. But that's in bad days. You know, some often did, used to go like out in the Genesee country. There you'd trash an hour before breakfast and then trash till dark. About 14 hours. About 12 hours is what they used.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you tell me?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Carl didn't want to admit his thrashing, huh?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, he'll tell me that he thrashed and he tells about it, but all I'm saying is he wouldn't say we were good thrashers, you know. He'd say, well, we thrashed.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: That's one thing I'd say. Carl and Oscar were two of the best around the country. Nobody could beat them. I don't care where you went, who thrashed. Now, Johnson was out there in the region. He was a pretty good thrasher too. But he couldn't come up to Old Fremont. My brother-in-law's dad, Andrew Hawkinson, he couldn't come up to them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do they, does that mean that they got a lot more work?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yes, and the job they done.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were they much in demand then? Did people want them to? Yes. They had as much as they could handle then?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: More than they could handle. You see, they used to take a little barrage and drive quick and up and around Plasmon Hill and clean it around. Well, then John Johnson started out there and then Andrew Hawkinson bought the second machine. He went out there, so then the Old Fremont took big barrage. So they went clean to lower end of Big Barrage. And then up on Dry Creek and ended up going up and around by Avon and clean it back, come clean around by Plasmon Hill. Hmm.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did this stuff end? What happened there to the thrashing? Why did it go out?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, they started in with these smaller machines like the 28 and 26 and these are gas thrashers and lots of people started doing thrashing. Then, now Carl, well Robert, no Carl too, Carl and Oscar, they got rid of their steam engine and they bought a smaller one and the Yardier or Case, Case gas tractor. And the same with Albert and Robert, Robert was one of them too in the last traction. And then the Combiners came in.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Carl told me that Robert really knew an awful lot about a lot of things. He said Robert is the one in the family that he sort of singles out as being a guy that studied and knew things, especially about mining. Just about anything you'd ask him, he said he'd have an answer.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You see, he took a course at the University of Mining. But when they come down to steam and machinery like thrashing, Oscar would take him there. See, Oscar, when Oscar came in to start a traction here, he ran shape for a P.F. for a partridge up in Elk Ridge.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's right, I've seen a picture of him.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, yeah. And then, so he knew all about steam then. And then he taught Carl to run the engine and then he ran the separator. But that's the end of traction, there was lots of little... Philarmonie, over here had a little traction outfit. Oscar and Carl had one. And John R. Johnson had a traction outfit. Charlie Smith had two.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, another thing about the Olsons is, from Carl, it just makes me think that those guys would be as honest as a day is long with all the work they were doing. I mean, I would think that they'd really give people a lot for, you know, do the best they could. Really put out a lot of effort.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, I'll tell you, that's one thing I say about it. Albert, he was kind of hot-headed though. Robert, he would go to Carl and the machine and Robert would get after him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you mean, crowd?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, it's trashing up too much grain. Oh, yeah. But Oscar, he took care of that for Robert. Carl didn't have to say anything because Oscar, which I think, shut up. He'd tell him what Carl had done. Carl was told about it, getting enough sacks, but Oscar, he shut up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did you tell me that once that Carl... well, Carl's mentioned to me too. Once he got really mad at his teacher and he quit school.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He got mad at Guy Kitts.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He got what?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He got mad at Guy Kitts. Guy Kitts, you know him? No. He'd make me panic and pull my teeth to live over here where the house is.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This guy's father? This guy's father, right?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: The guy, but...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did this guy do? Did he... was he giving Carl a hard time?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No, I don't know. They got in an argument in school about something. Carl had a temper and blew up. And they got in an argument and Carl took his books and went home. I was there when it happened.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that the last time Carl went to school?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Mm-hmm, last time he went to school. Guy tossed off him and he had a... he had a shoe string that he had to carry books in. He'd double it up and hit Guy with that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Carl did?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Mm-hmm, yeah. And then he told him that he was going and Guy tossed off him and he said, you can't toss him in here with that man. And they had to answer Carl. Carl just took his books and went home. That's the last time. Now, Carl had a temper. He'll ask if he gets an argument. If he gets a good argument, Carl, he... I see him get mad a lot of times. He can't stand argument, you know? He figure he's... he's going to win. That's why. And now Oscar was absolutely the other way. You couldn't... I don't think you could cut an argument out of Oscar.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oscar, he died young, didn't he?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, he was young when he died. See what happened to Oscar. He ran around them shades on them rough side spurs up there, shaking. And he took one kidney loose. And those days they didn't know enough to operate. They got a kidney, so I think it was cancelled, the kidney… he died… he suffered. Oh boy, that man. I'll tell you, I was up there and I seen him when he used Grey's Teeth to tell people.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Grey's Teeth, so what?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Grey's Teeth. Oh. He used for the pain. Yeah. Guys went up there, round here lots. He liked to play cards, he used to go up there and play poker and rummy and different games. He said draw all night till the next daylight. Pastime with him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This is when he was sick, eh? Yeah. Where was he then? Was he still there?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well he had...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The home place?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, just right across, you know where Danny McKenzie got his trade house. Just across the road back on the hill there was a cabin. That's the place they're calling Oscar, well Oscar bought that when he come out and he been calling for him. And then he got bad so then he had to move in over there where Amel is, the folks. That's where he died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he have it for a long time before he finally died?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oscar suffered for... Must have been three years anyway. He suffered with that. I forget just how old Oscar was, but he wasn't old when he died. He couldn't have been older than his 30s.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember the parents? Their parents? Mr. and Mrs. Wolfe? Yeah.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh you see, in the neighborhood.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Seems like they raised quite a family.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They did. Always told. It's our children. Your family. And off the damn notes, two boys, Carl Neimo and Ida and Amel, three girls. One girl dead.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember with the father, Mr. Olson, he worked? Do you remember about his work and what he did?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He worked on the sawmill for the Troy Lumber Company. That's where he worked. He was a sawmill man.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Which one of his sons was he like? Do you remember? I mean if you were going to say, was he like... Which one of the boys took after him?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I don't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'm just trying to know a little what he was like.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh, Wolfen, he was a good-natured guy. Full of fun. He was a joker. Wolfen, he wasn't like Carl or Albert or any of them. No, I don't know any of the boys really. Axel, the oldest boy, Axel and Oscar I guess would be about the closest.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, you know, the other thing I wanted to ask you about too was about the way that the farming is changing. You were talking to me about some before and I really got the idea that the way you see it, it's really ruining the land, the way they're farming. Now why?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, one thing you can take this nitrate. You ain't putting that little pellet in the ground. Well, we used to plow under clover, probably red clover that high, building up the soil. You filled the soil so you couldn't wash. You had something there, green manure crop. Yeah, I raised on red clover. That's what Amal Olsen tell you too. We raised just some good wheat crops on red clover ground as they raise now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you get the same kind of yield?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, all here without any other. I raised 60 books of wheat on it. And we didn't have no gains wheat like we got now. We had different kinds of wheat, 40 fold. And oh God, there were so many strains of wheat. But we never had no gains. If we'd had a gains wheat, we could have had our 80 books of wheat too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, now when you say...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I'll tell you, you see now when you plow, you don't see these little humus stringers in the ground.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The humus in the ground?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, you don't see that anymore. These little stringers, just like webs when you plow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean after you plow you'd see that?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You could see that in your furrow when your plow is going. You could see it. But you don't see that no more. That's your life, your fiber has gone out of the soil. And that ground, of course we didn't dry plow like we do now, but that ground would turn up just like a nice garden.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean when you were...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: When we plowed, yeah. When we re-sinked over. And like now, you take and go down now and see your ground. You go down 12 inches now. Look what you're turning up. Red hard soil. In those days, it hadn't washed off. You had good, rich soil right down. I walked in furrow up to here. I had a foot burner and had good soil.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You walking soil halfway up to your knee?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Falling in the foot burner. Oh, we plowed. We plowed up to 14 inches.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, I didn't know that.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They say shallow plowing like they do. It's not 18 inches. They didn't believe in that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And it was good soil clear, clear down?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yes. And I can show you spots like around the south side of this field here. Down on the curve down there. And over across on the field furrow over. It's rock. And we could plow 14 inches deep. And never even know there was rock there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What happened to the soil?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It washed off. And then plowed down the hill all the time. Plowed it off.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And washed off because it hasn't...

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Then you take a few years to keep it plowed down the hill. Every time you plow 16 inches. Say now you plow 16 inches wide and 8 inches deep. Well, you have turned that soil completely over. You're going to set up an edge. All right? You know that's going to make it... And on the side of the hill, that'll probably go out there 20 inches. Well, that makes a 10-ton soil. And the year after you plow down off the hill, that way you're going to get a 10-ton soil.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how did you rotate it? Did you have a first row of crop and then grow clover or fallow it? Or how did you do it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, we plow under our clover and then put that into fall wheat. And then I'll probably go back with peas and barley. Rotate it. Rotate it like that. And then after I got my D4 and 49, and I got a whole lot of these big chisels. You've probably seen them. They're real chisels, what they call them. I had them high beams, three, two, three. Well, I had three of them. And I went down 18 inches and broke up the bottom. As Andy Hilliard said when he rented my place then when I quit in 62, he said you could tell the difference on plowing here than on his that hadn't been chiseled.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the difference?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Plow leisure. And you could see for years, I don't know if of course you could know, for years you could see where that chiseled area was. Well, you see a crack along there in the bottom of your furrow. And then I went around my hills this way. Said, good boy, I should have run right into it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You sort of contoured it.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Contoured it good. Never to get anything that could run. If I had a corner like over on that field over here, I'd go forth and back there, and I'd get up far enough so I could go around the whole side of the hill. And I'd done that every third year.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Every third year? You chiseled it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I chiseled it every third year. This place here, I didn't get any of it. It wasn't chiseled three times.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think it helped hold the soil besides making it easier to plow, having chiseled it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, I bet you because that water went right down there, cleaned down to the chiseling forest. It couldn't go like you plow eight inches now. Once I do, the water comes and springs down to that, what you call it, plow soil. Then it runs there, and then it gets up by the water and you just take that root with it. You couldn't do that with the chiseling. And then we plowed down the clover. You had all of that there to hold it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did they start with this fertilizing, the kind they're doing now?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They started it in the...we didn't use it here until in the 50s, late 50s. They started with it down there on the Walla before because Fred Greenville, he used to farm this place, Fredman Place, and he had a friend down there, a schoolmate, and he'd been using it and he tried three different years to germinate clover on that nitrate ground and could get a germination. So that fellow told him, he says, you use that, he says, you can't even start raising grass and keep on plowing. It takes everything there is out of the soil. All you use is that pellet, dope. I'll tell you, when that first came out, I belonged to the Soil Conservation since 1930, and we had a meeting up here at Hawkinson's and there was many old stuff from Kendrick and so on from the NSC were there. And then they told all of us there, well, he says, just like you get sick, you're shot in the arm, you're worse off after it dies away. And that's what's going to happen to your nitrate, they told us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They were telling you not to use it then?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They were again. You're missing nitrate. Gosh, he used to come up here every, oh, go through the country, he'd always stop in here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's his name?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Manny Ohnstadt. He lives right across from the Kendrick screw house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is he retired?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: He's retired. He's an oral conservation man. Damn good one too. Manning was good.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you think it's the fertilizing that's really the cause of the ruining?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No, you take that and it's contour work, that's what they taught us, not to plow rock the field and work it down the hills and everything. Contour, seed contour, that's one thing that's what they were for. And you see lots of that going on too now. People are getting more careful about their seeding.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think they like your fields here in a lot worse shape now than they were when you were?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They're played out from that nitrate, getting played out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can you see it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You can tell by how the ground works up, sure. It's hard, the ground's getting harder. And you take and go out and all, right? Well, it'll go out on the lower end of Macquarie, you know, out that way. And go out to the Gen Z. You see them hills. You ever have a chance on some of that ground, you can find it just like pellets, just like it was gravel. That's what it starts to get like. It gets played out. And after that, you ain't got much left. Now there was a fellow by the name of Williams, he come from Kansas, and he was here in Moscow for seven years. He was selling combines for Farbrook. And he went back there, and he came here that fall. And he said there was just a plot to three towns for dead, and people had moved to Alaska and couldn't raise a thing. You can't even hear a midgrass. And Stanley Hilliard, when his uncle and auntie died in eastern Montana, he went into western Minnesota, and he said, There was the same thing over there, a plot to it. Stanley can tell you about that. He told me. That's just what it was. Finally, it'll die out. Well, you see, you've heard and read now about what happened in Africa after they took all that timber and that folio. Where them people are starving. They can't raise anything, they're not. They took the vegetation off.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: By the way, do you think that that's why the creeks don't run here much anymore, like they used to? Is it because they cut the timber off the hill?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: That's absolutely it. Absolutely. This creek down here, Bright Creek, I could go down here and fish in an ice stream in July, in August. There was running water here the years round. Come from Springs and Etup and clean up in White Pine. Same Bear Creek. Bear Creek was a good stream. Come clean back from Sand Mountain and Micomine. And that was all timber. Snow lay there until in June. Now what have you got? Now when it goes, it all goes at one time. I don't care how deep the snow falls. Get our spring at toss and rain and sun and you're out of snow. And not defeated. No Bear Creek down here. I've seen the times in August when Bear Creek would be as wide as across this room here. Bright Creek down here, same way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's so darn hard for me to, you know, I mean I can see it, what you're saying, but it's so hard to imagine it, having never seen it myself.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: If you haven't seen it, you wouldn't believe it. You wouldn't believe what difference it is now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When did that start to happen? When did the creek start to go up?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well that started after they logged off Bear Creek, after they logged off all through Bear Creek, all the way from below Amal Olsen. And clean up to Moscow Mountain. And then log everything up here, clean up to the Moscow Mountain on this side.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think it'll change again if the timber grows back?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well how are you going to go back? Where they've been logging with these catties, nothing left. Have you ever been on the East Fork or Potlatch out of Bovill?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't think so.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You go up there and see what's left. Yes, it's ice sand timber. Now they've logged it three times, three, four times. And some of that they took down there. It's just one hill there, just bare. What they didn't take, they now go with the cats and skidding logs. It's a, already it's a fright to look at.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've seen, I've seen that kind of stuff. I've seen it, I've seen it up on near Ball Mountain where we had, I was a lookout.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, and you take the same route, you go up, clean up to the upper basin of Elk River. Go eastward, clean to the North Fork. A lot of Elk River. Go clean down south to the Clearwater. You've got the same thing. There. Park country back, a park back, A.P. Lewis was. Yes, one little spot there on, yes, they actually leave back a park there. Little standing timber, a white pine spot like this and dirt. But they'll be logging up pretty quick. Otherwise they're getting nothing there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why, why do you think all that happened? I mean, do you think they just were ignorant of it or they didn't care?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Why? Potlatch just wanted all the logs they could get off of there. And they're logging, not like with them cats, you know, you'd think about, well, you make a skid, you know, it'll go down. Well, you hook onto a tree here and you just take off wherever you want, right down through the tail. That'll fall ahead of you.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now when did they start logging on Bear Creek and all the way up to the mountain?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Bear Creek down here, when the potters come over, that was 1917. They logged down here. That's going back some pretty good. But then that was horse logging. That was different. You didn't run through the timber, you had to have a skidding road then. And that place over there in Park Country, Merton Pierce, he logged that with horses and this. There's standing white pine trees and there's not much of it there on Middle Creek. But you take down, go back in where they started with these big cats, you don't see much left. And now them trees are standing, they can't take the wind. Lots of them like to camp back now. They're starting to die.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what's going on? It sounds like they're ruining the country.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, I'll tell you... the state and the federal government. Why did they allow that to be happening on their land? That pot must take over, beat them hard. Why? Why didn't they make them be careful about the logging? Now you hear about up there in Hell Canyon, they don't make them do it with helicopter. Because they don't want to tear off the timber. But they should have made them be more careful with their cats not to run down the little trees that they did up there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But you know, you got two, you got the first the woods and then the farms too. It sounds like the soil. The soil is going to Hell too. You know, you ruin the farms and you ruin the timber. What have you got left?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You ruin the timber for a watershed and after that there goes your farming with it. Now you don't see much good summer rains like we used to have. We have no moisture for it. Like last summer, look how dry and hot they got. Well, when I was a kid and many, many years after, you didn't see that. You didn't see that they're hot. They're like that. We had our thunderstorms of course, but never no periods like we've been having lately. Get worse every year. Now you take our two last years, you know how we used to be around for two years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Three years.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: All right. You see now it's been dry and hot. And that, I'll go back, I'll go back at least 10 years or less and it's a difference.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how was it 50 years ago in the summer? Was it, was it not, it wasn't, it wasn't so dry and hot as it is now?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It's, it's way different, way different. I'll tell you, it's in June, you could always look at it, last part of May, June when cops are wanting to have good rains. Mids around mids around mids, 40 July, always you'd have good rains. Never missed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what is, I mean, do you think that they're, that they have something to do not having rain has got something to do with cutting the timber? Is that it or?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Cutting the timber down? Well, you figure then, oh, when like I told you about up here, no, well up in White Point, Moscow Mountain, you can find snow there in the North, up there in June. Well, that was still the feeding of streams, moisture in the air. Now when there's no snow up there, there's nothing to get from in June.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, you really think that, like that moisture in the air itself helps cause the rain to come?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Sure, and the streams now, like you take Troy Creek, the one down here by Olke Olsen, one Spring Valley, Dry Creek, Bear Creek and all the Potlatch, all of them are running with water. You see, the sun has something to draw moisture from. Now it don't have it. Not Dry Creek, but Plum Dry last year. Sure it did. All but what was feeding from the spring down here, from the spring down with some water.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You think that it's, you know, I was thinking that because our hills aren't as high, let's say they're, you know, what, they're only 4,000 feet, you know, and around there, as the ones are south of here, like off the Clearwater, south of Clearwater where you got 8,000 feet, I suppose that would make a big difference too. We don't have as much, it gets drier earlier around here because our hills are a lot lower. You don't have as much snow staying as late anyway.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, you take, now you go in there now, like after in June and July fishing. Well, up in Marlborough Creek, up across there by Lost Lake, I know where we couldn't go in there last year, you know, the kind of snowdrifts. Now you can go in there on the dusty road. And Marlborough Creek, I'll tell you, Marlborough Creek was small last year. Surprising. Marlborough Creek knows, I seen Potlatch Creek down here, but Kendrick Creek and Marlborough Creek. You think going back to horse logging would be a good way to... With the cats, not to just go and hook onto a tree, you could, now they got winch on all that stuff, winch them out. They said, pull them, go in there with the cat, right through their small timber. Once when you have a chance, go up on East Fork out of Potlatch, go clean up there to the divide that leads into Upper Basin. And then also out of Elk River, go on the Diamond Road to, down to where Bulls Cabin used to be. And you can just see for yourself just what it's like.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You told me that Indians kept this country burnt off. It seems like maybe they knew what they were doing.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I'll tell you, by God, there's more than one that'll agree with me that Indians have better care than we do. Where did they get these big white pines up to six feet across there, and all this big pine timber that was here, taking care of the timber, no infestation. Now you can't grow a tree like that, it'll die before it gets that big.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So probably the burning kept the disease out.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, you betcha. And there was no underbrush or small trees standing scrubbing underneath there. It was all burnt off.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder how they burnt, or when they burnt.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: They burnt out in the summer when it got dry. They set a grass fire.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would they set it down a ridge and burn it up?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I'll tell you, they burned the whole country. They burned the whole country. This country, Dad's Hibbett, burnt all the way from here clean up to North of Bogle and around. Why should a grass fire never gotten a big fire, did it?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I wonder if there was any way to figure out when they stopped burning. What about when they stopped? I suppose it was when your father came, they were still burning. So probably stopped some not too long after.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, after the homesteader got in here, the Indians got over on the reservation that stopped it. After they drove them on the reservation, they wasn't traveling through. So that started quite a way back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And what about the farming? What could you do about, if you stopped using fertilizer now, could you bring the soil back?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, you'd have to go back to, just like Donald Porter was talking here today, do a fertilizer getting out, getting a high price, you're going to have to go back to Kroger or something. Try to do something else.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you tell me once that you could see the places where it's not being farmed, where you can see the color of the grass as being different?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: You can tell the difference, where you haven't used fertilizer. If you had a place there, well, I'll tell you. I'll take my two acre garden here against a field that goes all around it and I'll show you the difference. I'll show you what I got in the garden, I got good soil.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Or seeded.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Of course that was from using straw manure in that one, it's building up the ground. I'm not going to have manure or anything anymore, I don't know what it's going to be because it's going to run together on me. I want to figure it out, take off a piece of garden each year and put it into rape and plow under. Rape is a good thing to break up the soil. I've seen rape roots, Oscar Hawkins had seven acres up there and he was plowing eight inches deep. And we took off a root that big at the bottom, that long, pulled out of the bottom. So that much is what I see, you can figure that was over 20 inches long. Now that'll open up the bottom of the soil. And you take them little roots now, some of them are that big, when they're out there, there's something to build up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's probably about almost two inches around, two inches in diameter.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well that's something, you get that thick in the ground, Oscar had the furrow for white when he plowed it, all that to fill up the soil. Rape, I'll tell you, is a good thing to build up soil, which is anything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They've been using that lately, hasn't it?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah, and it's a sheep to put a duet that of course they don't cost you nothing. Oscar, he bought two pounds an acre and paid eight cents an acre, 16 cents an acre to seed it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's great, that's great.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well soil builder, you get out of it too. And you put that in the fall and then you plow the next year. So you don't have to lay your ground over like you would with lots of other things, I'll fowl for that. You've got a four week ground next year again.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: One other thing I want to ask you about was the cemetery on Dry Ridge here. Now I've heard, I mean it's a beautiful place.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It is. It's supposed to be the nicest cemetery around the country. Well now normally the British folks, when they bought the hotel down here, run the hotel down there, they went to all the end of the sea and all of Moscow and all over leftover and showed Dry Ridge to be buried in. That's where they're buried, Norman folks. That was the prettiest cemetery. So you can see, outsiders come through, give it to credit.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know about when the cemetery got going? Was it there when you were a little kid?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh Jesus, that was going in the 1800s. I don't know when the first one was buried up there. That's way back. And the graves up there, nobody knows anything about. Lost and forgotten. Now there's two next to the folks up there. Eddie Sorsen got the book and he sold that lot to Clarence Johnson when his father died. Dad told him not to take that lot because Master and Mrs. Melgret, they homestead this place, Sanctuary, right across the gang. So when she died she asked dad to take care of their lot because the boy went back east. So we did it, well I did, until I seeded it into grass. And they started digging down there, Morris Harland Dorsey started digging. They came out one box and then they came out another. So then Clarence had to buy a lot down there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How come they didn't know that there was somebody buried there?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It should be in the book. Every lot was marked in that book. There's lots of it that's up there. I have several lost friends. They're going to find themselves finding cask boxes down there after a few years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well now I've heard that it's hard to dig in the ground there too, is that true?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh boy. You get down there towards the last, last of that grave there you stick a sharp pick and drive it as hard as you can. You stick on there and you get about that much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is this all year round? It's hard to...?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: It's that way all the time. It's a blue heart of hand. Now Blink, he does pretty good with that digging machine. He does pretty good at it. But when you go and do it by hand, boy, four men a day you will carve it into the grave.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Four men a whole day?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Shaped around two and two.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you dug graves up there?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: I don't say I haven't. I've dug lots of them. And what we used to do, Carl Olsen used to be with us up there too, set a hole on there, two on the center and one over here and shoot them all at one time. You get a hole probably that big around, it'll open down through and then in between you've got a break to do it with the pick.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean you use dynamite?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yeah. You can't shoot the whole grave. You shoot the whole grave here and there. And you've got to work the rest of it up. But that gives you a chance to pick against that then. I know, you used to have sharp edges, you know what they are. You used to have that there. You'd have to use a knife and drive that to your side and then you had to take it off with your hand because it stuck on the edge of the pick. It's sticky.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is it true that in the summer you can see where people are buried sometimes?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Now I drive to what's called Fall Beach up there and I forget who's up there, I show them my new where they were buried. Mrs. Peterson, that's inside the portal and then it's Mrs. Samberg, up here, her mother. And then it's Mrs. Cravey, used to own a place across the road. And then right down there across from my folks, there's Mrs. Young-Lindeman, which is a green spot right there. You can see a little bit of a swale there in the center of the driveway. There's a gravel track on each side. It's a little, a short little off the grave there. You can tell that fall is the size of the grave I buried here. So there must be gas coming up from the grave.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You can see there's other places in the cemetery too, just where it stays greener?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, there's other out here, it's mold all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you can't tell there?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: No, you can't tell there. The only ones I could tell were the cemetery.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The ones right on the road?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: And you can stand at one end of the cemetery and look up the road and see the graves down through there, that fall. No less, even I was up there and I forgot some other people up there. Then I started talking about that. I know some and they didn't know anything about it, just then I mentioned about it through his very death.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you think it is that the birds and those people find so beautiful about the cemetery? I think it's beautiful, but I'm wondering why it's so, is it the trees that are there? It's just something about it, it's lovely.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, I'll tell you, you take on Brecker Cemetery nowadays, they have a lot of shade trees up there. I took them all out. They had some red firs up there, some dead, and I took them all out there. Light like bushes, another thing we dug out. Got them light like bushes, you know, they'd push tombstones over. Oh really? Yeah, one of the people in any other bank could have been in there. Frank was, he took chances.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Does that mean that he was better to the people?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Yep, I'll say that for Frank. Actually, if we don't hear that, I'm going to tell you something. I don't want no take for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Okay, but tell me, I didn't get that. You really do think that Frank has been the best man?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: That's what I say, Frank is the best one we've had in Troy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about during the hard times in the depression? Did the bank help people?

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Oh yes, that was Wally Bowman then. He helped the people.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I guess I should get going.

speaker: Elmer Flodin
words: Well, you go up and see Otto Osterberg and you're going to get it. Frank? Frank Brocke, I'll tell you, done a lot for the people.
